The RS latch is constructed of two cross-coupled NOR gates. The feedback lines extend from the outputs of each gate and connect to an input leg of the opposite gate.
The two inputs are SET (S) and RESET (R) and the two outputs are Q and Q. Remember that when the latch is SET it means that
Q is 1 and Q is 0. When the latch is RESET, Q is 0 and Q is 1.
To understand the operation of the RS latch we will examine all of its possible input combinations.
When power is first applied, the latch will normally assume some output condition, meaning Q will either be HIGH or it will be LOW, and Q will be the inverse of Q.f Q.................
For simplicity, assume the latch will have no output. As we step through its operations, we will fill in its truth table. not change. This condition is labeled in the truth table as NO CHANGE.

The first inputs applied are S = 0 and R = 0. Since the inputs of a NOR gate need a HIGH input to produce a LOW output, the outputs of the latch do not change. This condition is labeled in the truth table as "NO CHANGE". If the flip-flop had started in the RESET state, it would stay in the RESET state with this input.

0 0 NO CHANGE
The next inputs are S = 0 and R = 1. This is the RESET input. As soon as the HIGH is applied to the top NOR gate, the Q output goes LOW.ally goes LOW.
The LOW is sent via the feedback line to the upper leg of the bottom NOR gate. With two LOW inputs, the Q output goes HIGH, placing the latch in a RESET condition.. in a RESET condition.
Notice that if the HIGH is now removed from the RESET input, the latch will not change - it will, in effect, remember its last state.....
The next inputs are S = 1 and R = 0. This is the SET input. When a HIGH is applied to the lower NOR gate, the output goes LOW.
0 0 NO CHANGE
That LOW is then transferred to the upper gate through the feedback line, putting two LOWs on the upper gate. This forces the Q output HIGH and that, in turn, places the latch in the SET condition.

Under normal operating conditions, this problem will never occur, but it can occur as an indirect result of placing the INVALID input combination on the latch.

What makes the INVALID input combination so undesirable is that it sets up the latch for what is called RACE condition.

RACE condition is when the two gates are both trying to go HIGH at the same time and literally race against each other until one of them goes HIGH first, latching the other gate LOW. The problem is that it's entirely unpredictable...

One of the driving forces behind the development of the RS latch was to create a "bounceless" electronic switch with the ability to switch between HIGH and LOW without the contact bounce inherent in mechanical switches...

When a mechanical switch is operated, there is always some degree of contact bounce. The diagram below shows the effect of the bounce on a digital signal.W without the contact bounce inherent in mechanical switches...

Notice that switching from one position to the other actually produces several voltage spikes before the switch contact comes to rest. While the period of bounce may only last a few milliseconds, in digital circuits this is an eternity of havoc.avoc...
When a latch is employed, the effect of contact bounce is eliminated. Let's look at an example. This switch is in its normal position, holding the latch in a RESET condition.

When the switch is moved, it applies 5 volts to the S input. The switch will still bounce, but the latch will become SET during the very first contact of the switch. All successive bounces will be ignored because the device has already latched into the SET condition.ssive bounces will be ignored because the device has already latched into the SET condition.

Since the NAND latch works opposite from the NOR latch, we'll begin analysis from the bottom of the truth table.

When the input condition of R=1 and S=1 is applied to the latch there is no change or hold condition. Since both inputs are inhibited, they are active low. This results in no action occurring in the latch. This is the NO CHANGE or HOLD state...te..te.
1 1 NO CHANGE

The next input combination is S = 1 and R = 0. This is the RESET input. As soon as the LOW is applied to the bottom NAND gate, its output automatically goes HIGH. The HIGH is sent via the feedback line to the bottom leg of the upper NAND gate.
With two HIGH inputs, the upper NAND gate goes LOW. The LOW on the output of the upper NAND gate feeds back to the lower gate, latching in a RESET condition.
1 1 NO CHANGE

The next input combination is S = 0 and R = 1. This is the SET input. As soon as the LOW is applied to the upper NAND gate, the output goes HIGH. The HIGH is sent via the feedback line to the upper leg of the lower NAND gate.
With two HIGH inputs, the lower NAND gate goes LOW. The LOW on the output of the lower NAND gate feeds back to the upper gate, latching in a SET condition.?
1 1 NO CHANGE
The last input combination is S = 0 and R = 0. This is the INVALID input condition. In this state, both NAND gates receive a LOW input. This forces both gates to output HIGHs.
Just as with the RS latch, this output condition is INVALID and should be avoided for the same reasons.
